title: The Woman Made of Light: Fullersburg, the Serpentine, and the Lamps of the Folies Bergère
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Fullersburg, Illinois, birth on the farm
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia gives 15 January 1862 at Fullersburg; the French article's infobox agrees while its running text gives 22 January 1862 at Hinsdale, a contradiction internal to that source and not resolved here
stops.campa: On a farm in the settlement of Fullersburg, west of Chicago, a daughter is born to the Fuller family and named Marie Louise. The place is a mill hamlet on Salt Creek that the growing towns will later swallow, so that later accounts give her birthplace as Hinsdale and later still as Oak Brook, and no two of them agree on the day. She discards the given name early, answering to Loie, and later spells it with a French dieresis. The child born on this prairie will spend her working life indoors, in the dark, teaching electric light to behave like weather.
suggested_refs: The Graue Mill and the vanished settlement of Fullersburg, Salt Creek, now Oak Brook, Illinois

stops.name: Chicago, the boarding house and the Progressive Lyceum
stops.date_confidence: the move at about age two and the boarding house are attested; the Sunday recitation of 'Mary Had a Little Lamb' is reported only from her own memoir with no year attached, so the year here is editorial
stops.campa: The family gives up the country for the city and keeps a boarding house, a business of strangers' meals and strangers' talk. On Sunday mornings the child is taken not to a church but to the Progressive Lyceum, a free-thinkers' school where children speak in front of adults. She recites Mary Had a Little Lamb from the platform, in her own telling her first performance, and is not yet old enough to be shy of it. Chicago in these years is lumber and rail, filling with people faster than it can house them, and she grows up among lodgers who pay by the week.
suggested_refs: The Progressive Lyceum of Chicago, free-thinkers' Sunday school of her childhood

stops.name: Chicago Academy of Music, the child on the boards
stops.date_confidence: the debut in 'Was He Right?' is attested; the venue is demolished and its address is not confirmed in the reachable sources, so the pin marks the Loop theater district generally
stops.campa: At about four she is put on the stage of the Chicago Academy of Music in a play called Was He Right?, a formal debut for a child who has already learned that a room of adults will go quiet if she stands still first. The venue is gone and its exact address cannot be recovered from the reachable sources. The episode sets the shape of everything after it. She never enters a conservatory or a ballet class, and no teacher of any kind takes her on; her education is carried out from the start in front of paying strangers.
suggested_refs: The Chicago Academy of Music, site of her first billed dramatic role

stops.name: Chicago, out with the Vincent company
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Vincent company and the Aladdin pantomime; the Buffalo Bill engagement is given by the source only as 'around age nineteen'
stops.campa: She goes out with the Felix A. Vincent Company in a pantomime of Aladdin and enters the trade that will hold her for a decade: touring melodrama, burlesque, and spectacle, booked town by town across the middle of the country. There is no line in this work between acting, singing, and dancing, and a performer does whatever the bill needs. Around nineteen she joins Buffalo Bill Cody's touring act. The West that Cody sells to easterners is her workplace, not her homeland. She is learning the machinery of a show from inside it.
suggested_refs: The Felix A. Vincent Company touring repertory of the late 1870s

stops.name: New York, the melodrama years
stops.date_confidence: roles in 'Davy Crockett' (1882) and 'Twenty Days, or Buffalo Bill's Pledge' (1883) are attested; the sources name no other towns or parts across the decade
stops.campa: On the eastern half of the circuit she works the western melodramas that city audiences want: Davy Crockett, then Twenty Days, or Buffalo Bill's Pledge. She is a working actress of no particular fame, competent at everything and celebrated for nothing. The sources name almost none of the towns and none of the parts beyond these, so the decade stands in the record as a blank with a body moving through it. She acquires in it the one thing that will matter later, an exact knowledge of stage lamps, wings, gauzes, and the men who run them.
suggested_refs: The American melodrama and burletta circuit of the 1880s, in which she worked without notice

segments.name: London, the Silk, and the Serpentine

stops.name: London, Caprice fails
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is not given
stops.campa: She crosses to London to mount a play called Caprice and to star in it, her own production and her own gamble. It fails on both counts, critically and financially, and leaves her stranded in a city where nobody owes her a booking. The failure is complete enough that the next work she takes is understudy work at somebody else's house. She is twenty-seven and has been on a stage since she was four, with nothing to show for the years but the trade itself. The dance that will make her name does not exist yet, and nothing in this season predicts it.
suggested_refs: The London production of 'Caprice', 1889, her first attempt at management

stops.name: Gaiety Theatre, the skirt dance from the wings
stops.date_confidence: the understudy engagement and the exposure to skirt dancing are attested; the month is editorial
stops.campa: At the Gaiety Theatre in the Strand she takes an understudy's place and watches the house specialty from the wings: the skirt dance, an English music-hall form in which a woman in a wide skirt lifts and swings the fabric to catch the light. It is not deep art and nobody in London pretends it is. She takes from it the one idea she needs, that cloth in motion is what an audience watches and not the woman inside it. She carries the notion back across the Atlantic with no plan for what to do with it.
stops.quote: What is the dance? It is motion. What is motion? The expression of a sensation. What is a sensation? The reaction in the human body produced by an impression or an idea perceived by the mind.
stops.quote_source: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Chapter VI, 'Light and the Dance', Project Gutenberg #72257, written long after the Gaiety season
suggested_refs: The Gaiety Theatre, Strand, home of the English skirt dance

stops.name: Holyoke, Massachusetts, the silk in the gaslight
stops.date_confidence: the date and the Holyoke performance of 'Quack Medical Doctor' come from French Wikipedia, which treats the night as the origin of her style; her own memoir tells the discovery without a date
stops.campa: In a Massachusetts mill town she is playing in a farce called Quack Medical Doctor, hypnotized on stage and required to move as though under a spell. She has with her a length of light Indian silk, a gift from two English officers, far too long for her body. She lifts it and turns beneath the footlights and the house calls out that she is a butterfly, then an orchid. The French account treats this night as the birth of everything. Her own memoir describes the real discovery as something made afterwards, alone with the fabric, testing what light would do to it.
stops.quote: Gently, almost religiously, I set the silk in motion, and I saw that I had obtained undulations of a character heretofore unknown. I had created a new dance. Why had I never thought of it before?
stops.quote_source: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (London: Herbert Jenkins, 1913), Chapter III, 'How I Created the Serpentine Dance', Project Gutenberg #72257
suggested_refs: The Indian silk sent to her by two English officers, described in Chapter III of the memoir
sources: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Project Gutenberg #72257

stops.name: Casino Theatre, New York, the Serpentine is named
stops.date_confidence: the year, the venue, the manager, and the naming are attested; the month is editorial
stops.campa: Rudolph Aronson, who runs the Casino Theatre, sees the silk act and hires it to fill the space between the acts of a comedy called Uncle Celestin. He gives it a name, The Serpentine, and the name will outlive her. She dances the entr'acte in white silk lit from the wings through colored glass she has specified herself, and for the first time the effect is not a costume trick but a designed event. The comedy is forgotten within the year. What New York comes to see is the interval between its acts.
suggested_refs: The Casino Theatre, Broadway at 39th Street, where Aronson named the Serpentine Dance

stops.name: Madison Square Theatre, the engagement moves
stops.date_confidence: the move and the second success are attested; the often repeated cause, a quarrel with Aronson, appears in no source consulted and is carried here as tradition only
stops.campa: She moves the engagement across town to the Madison Square Theatre, where the success repeats. The reason for the move is not given in the reachable sources; a later tradition says she quarreled with Aronson, and it is recorded here without endorsement. The sources state only that she succeeded at both houses in the same season. She is not yet thirty and has built, out of a music-hall trick and a length of surplus silk, an act that within months a dozen other women are performing under her own title.
suggested_refs: The Madison Square Theatre, 24 West 24th Street, demolished

stops.name: Park Theatre, Brooklyn, the rival premiere
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia dates the premiere of the developed Serpentine Dance here; the English sources place the first performances at the Casino Theatre in 1891. Both accounts stand; the theater is demolished and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: The French account gives a different premiere: the fifteenth of February, at the Park Theatre in Brooklyn, where the fully worked Serpentine Dance is said to be shown for the first time. The English sources place the first performances at the Casino the previous autumn. Neither account is dropped here. Both agree that by the spring of 1892 the dance is loose in the world and being copied nightly in more than one city, while the woman who made it holds no paper on it at all.
suggested_refs: The Park Theatre, Brooklyn, long demolished, cited by French Wikipedia as the premiere house

stops.name: New York, Fuller v. Bemis
stops.date_confidence: the suit and the ruling are attested for 1892; the month is editorial
stops.campa: She sues Minnie Renwood Bemis, who performs the Serpentine Dance as her own, and asks the United States Circuit Court to stop her. The court refuses. Dance, it rules, tells no story; the Serpentine presents no dramatic narrative and so falls outside a copyright that protects only what can be read as a play. The decision hands her invention to any imitator with a bolt of silk. Eighty-four years later the Copyright Act of 1976 will extend protection to choreography that tells no story, and the case she lost is what the change is written against.
suggested_refs: Fuller v. Bemis (C.C.S.D.N.Y. 1892), the ruling that left choreography uncopyrightable

segments.name: Paris, and the Trade in Light

stops.name: Gare Saint-Lazare, Paris at last
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia dates her departure from America to June 1892; the memoir places the Paris arrival after failed engagements in Berlin, Altona, and Cologne, in October. The arrival point is not recorded and the station pin is a reasonable guess only
stops.campa: She leaves the country that will not protect her work, and after failed engagements in Berlin, Altona, and Cologne, where she danced in a circus between an elephant and a donkey, she arrives in Paris. No source records where she came in, so the station is a guess and nothing more. She has one act, no engagement, and no French. In the memoir she writes twenty years afterwards the city is not a destination at all but a rescue, a harbor reached out of weather she had been in for years.
stops.quote: Paris! Paris! At last Paris! It seemed to me that I was saved and that all my troubles were coming to an end. Paris was the port after storm, the harbour of refuge after the furious rage of life's tempest.
stops.quote_source: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Chapter V, 'My Appearance at the Folies-Bergère', Project Gutenberg #72257
suggested_refs: The German and Rhineland engagements of 1892, recounted in Chapter V of the memoir
sources: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Project Gutenberg #72257

stops.name: Folies Bergère, the imitator already booked
stops.date_confidence: the episode is Fuller's own account in the memoir; the day is editorial
stops.campa: She presents herself at the Folies Bergère on the rue Richer and finds the house already advertising a serpentine dance, performed by a woman who copied her in New York. Through her interpreter she asks the manager Marchand why. Because the Casino de Paris is announcing one, he answers, and he cannot let them get ahead of him. She buys out the imitator's contract and goes on under the imitator's billing. Marchand, she learns later, has understood every word of English spoken in front of him.
stops.quote: "I engaged this dancer," replied M. Marchand in French, "because the Casino de Paris is announcing a serpentine dance and because I cannot afford to let them get ahead of me."
stops.quote_source: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Chapter V, Project Gutenberg #72257
suggested_refs: Édouard Marchand's management of the Folies Bergère, 32 rue Richer
sources: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Project Gutenberg #72257

stops.name: Folies Bergère, the debut night
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia places the Folies Bergère engagement in the early 1890s and French Wikipedia gives no debut date; November 1892 is a reconstruction and should be read as such
stops.campa: The debut runs to five dances. By the fourth the house is standing, and the orchestra's prelude to the fifth cannot be heard through the noise. Paris has seen skirt dancing before. It has not seen a woman vanish inside several hundred square feet of moving silk lit from four directions by lamps she has aimed herself. Within the season she is among the highest paid performers alive and the theatre is selling her image on its posters. The draughtsmen of the new ornamental style begin arriving at the rue Richer with sketchbooks.
stops.quote: The enthusiasm of the audience grew progressively while I danced. When the curtain fell after the fourth dance, the applause was deafening and the music that served as prelude to dance number five could not be heard.
stops.quote_source: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Chapter V, Project Gutenberg #72257
suggested_refs: The Folies Bergère programs and posters of the 1892 to 1893 seasons
sources: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Project Gutenberg #72257

stops.name: Folies Bergère, the glass floor and the Fire Dance
stops.date_confidence: the mechanism, a glass floor with colored gels beneath, is attested; no source consulted attaches a year to it, and the placement here is reconstruction
stops.campa: For the Fire Dance she has the stage floor cut and glazed, a pane set into the boards with colored lamps beneath it, and she stands on the light itself. From the house she is a figure standing inside a column of flame that climbs her own skirts. No year is fixed for it in the reachable sources. It becomes the piece by which the century remembers her, and by now every element of it is hers: a machine she designed, a garment she cut, gels she mixed, on a stage she has persuaded a music hall to rebuild.
stops.quote: If I have been the first to employ coloured light, I deserve no special praise for that. I cannot explain the circumstance; I do not know how I do it... It is a matter of intuition, of instinct, and nothing else.
stops.quote_source: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Chapter VI, Project Gutenberg #72257, written two decades after the Fire Dance
suggested_refs: The illuminated glass stage floor built for the Fire Dance at the Folies Bergère

stops.name: Washington, the patents filed
stops.date_confidence: the patent numbers 513102, 518347, and 533167 are attested and fall in the 1894 to 1895 issue range; French Wikipedia dates the costume patent to 1894. Earlier accounts giving 1893 are not supported by the numbers
stops.campa: She files in Washington on everything she has built: a garment for dancers, a mechanism for the production of stage effects, a theatrical stage mechanism, and alongside them chemical formulas for salts that hold light and give it back in the dark. Something like ten patents and deposits are made in these years in Washington and Paris. She is a dancer who does not perform an invention so much as patent a performance. None of it recovers what the Bemis ruling gave away, because the thing everyone copies is the one thing no office will register.
suggested_refs: US patents 513102 (Mechanism for the Production of Stage Effects), 518347 (Garment for Dancers), 533167 (Theatrical Stage Mechanism)

stops.name: West Orange, New Jersey, the camera takes the dance
stops.date_confidence: the Edison Studios film 'Annabelle Serpentine Dance' is attested for 1895 and the Lumière version for 1896; the West Orange studio pin is approximate and not confirmed in the reachable sources
stops.campa: At Thomas Edison's studio in New Jersey a dancer named Annabelle Whitford is filmed performing the serpentine, and the print is tinted by hand, frame by frame, to counterfeit the colored light Fuller pours out of her lamps. The Lumière brothers shoot their own version in France the following year. Neither film is of her. The new medium takes up her invention within four years of its own birth and takes it from somebody else, exactly as the theaters did, so that the surviving moving images of the Serpentine Dance are images of her imitators.
suggested_refs: Edison Studios, 'Annabelle Serpentine Dance' (1895), hand-tinted; the Lumière serpentine film (1896)

stops.name: Paris, colour is disintegrated light
stops.date_confidence: the theoretical statement survives only in the 1908 memoir, written years after the practice it describes, so the placement in this year is editorial; her membership of the Société astronomique de France is attested by French Wikipedia from 1895, and accounts placing it in the 1900s are wrong
stops.campa: Between engagements she writes out what she thinks she is doing. Colour, she says, is disintegrated light. Motion is the expression of a sensation, and dance is nothing else. The theory reaches print only in the memoir, so its placement in this year is editorial, but the practice it describes is already running six nights a week. She keeps a workroom of dyes, gels, and luminous salts and tests fabrics against lamps. Then she denies that any of it is deliberate and calls it intuition and instinct. She has been a member of the Société astronomique de France since 1895.
stops.quote: Colour is disintegrated light. The rays of light, disintegrated by vibrations, touch one object and another, and this disintegration, photographed in the retina, is always chemically the result of changes in matter and in beams of light.
stops.quote_source: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Chapter VI, 'Light and the Dance', Project Gutenberg #72257
suggested_refs: Chapter VI of the memoir, 'Light and the Dance', her only sustained statement of theory
Membership rolls of the Société astronomique de France from 1895
sources: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Project Gutenberg #72257

segments.name: Gab, the Fullerets, and the Exposition

stops.name: Paris, living with Gabrielle Bloch
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia places their meeting in the mid-1890s without a year and gives 1898 for the beginning of cohabitation; the often repeated 1895 start date is manufactured precision
stops.campa: Gabrielle Bloch has been at her side since the middle of the decade, and from this year the two women live together. They will not be separated for thirty years. Bloch manages the company, the money, and the tours; in time she takes the name Gab Sorère and directs films at Fuller's side. The sources agree on the fact of the partnership and give no start date beyond the mid-1890s, so the length of it is better documented than its beginning. Everything Fuller makes after this year, she makes with her.
suggested_refs: Gabrielle Bloch, later Gab Sorère, manager, partner, and co-director

stops.name: Neuilly-sur-Seine, the school of the Fullerets
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the house and the school west of Paris come from general biographical accounts and were not confirmed against a named source in this pass; the address is unknown and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: West of Paris she keeps a house and a school, and trains a company of young women she calls the Fullerets to work silk and light as an ensemble rather than as solo turns. The address is not recoverable from the reachable sources and the pin is approximate. She does not teach steps. She teaches timing against a lamp, and the discipline of disappearing inside a garment so completely that an audience watches the fabric and never once looks for the face. The serpentine had been a solo; here it is drilled for a dozen bodies at once.
suggested_refs: The Fullerets, Fuller's company of trained young dancers, western suburbs of Paris
sources: general biographical accounts of Fuller's Paris-area residence and school, not independently verified in this pass

stops.name: Rue de Paris, her own theatre at the Exposition
stops.date_confidence: the théâtre-musée at the 1900 Exposition Universelle is attested by French Wikipedia; its exact footprint on the Rue de Paris attractions strip is not fixed and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: At the Exposition Universelle she has a building of her own, a small theatre on the attractions strip of the Rue de Paris with a plaster facade modeled on her own drapery in motion. Inside it she performs and shows her collection. No other performer at the fair is given a house shaped like herself. The fair draws visitors by the tens of millions, and a share of them pay to stand in the dark in front of her lamps, eight years after she arrived in this city with one act and no French.
suggested_refs: The Théâtre Loïe Fuller, Rue de Paris, Exposition Universelle of 1900

stops.name: The Exposition Universelle, Isadora Duncan comes in
stops.date_confidence: attested in the atlas record of Isadora Duncan's own 1900 visit to the fairground, Rodin's pavilion, and Fuller's theatre
stops.campa: Isadora Duncan, young and unknown, walks the fairground from Rodin's plaster pavilion to the little theatre with the drapery facade and sees inside it the thing she has been reaching for alone: a body dissolved into moving light. She has no company, no money, and a conviction that dance can be made out of nothing but the body's own impulse. Two years from now the woman performing here will put her on a train and pay for the concerts that make her name across Europe, and will then be eclipsed by her.
suggested_refs: Rodin's independent pavilion at the Place de l'Alma, 1900, and Fuller's theatre on the Rue de Paris

stops.name: Rue de Paris, presenting Sada Yacco
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia attests that Fuller introduced Sada Yacco to French audiences at her Exposition theatre in 1900; English Wikipedia says only that Fuller 'supported' her. The month is editorial and the word 'mentor', common in later accounts, overstates the record
stops.campa: She brings the Japanese actress Sada Yacco to her own theatre at the fair and presents her to Paris, where the Kawakami company's performances become one of the events of the season. Sada Yacco is already a star on two continents and is nobody's pupil; what Fuller supplies is a stage and an audience. She does this more than once in her life. She has an eye for performers who fit none of the available categories, having fit none of them herself, and she spends her own standing on them.
suggested_refs: The Kawakami company's 1900 Paris season, presented at Fuller's Exposition theatre

segments.name: The Tour, the Princess, and the Radium

stops.name: Paris, cast in gilt bronze
stops.date_confidence: Larche's gilt bronze is dated circa 1901; the 1893 Toulouse-Lautrec lithograph is firm, while the 1892 and 1901 dates for other images come from picture captions rather than article text and are held loosely
stops.campa: Raoul Larche casts her in gilt bronze as a lamp, the drapery rising off her lifted arms in a spiral with the bulb hidden inside the folds, so that the sculpture of the woman who dances in light is itself a light. Jules Chéret has already put her on posters and Toulouse-Lautrec made his lithograph of her in 1893. Koloman Moser draws her in Vienna. She is by now among the most reproduced bodies in Europe, and almost none of the reproductions show her face.
suggested_refs: François-Raoul Larche, 'Loïe Fuller, the Dancer', gilt bronze lamp, c. 1901, Museum Wiesbaden and the National Gallery of Australia

stops.name: Berlin, the touring company goes out
stops.date_confidence: attested in the atlas record of Isadora Duncan's journey, which fixes the Fuller invitation and the tour launch in March 1902
stops.campa: She has watched Isadora Duncan dance in a small Paris studio and makes her an offer: a European tour through Germany and Austria-Hungary, in Fuller's company, at Fuller's expense. The tour goes out in the spring. Fuller is the draw and Fuller pays the bills, and the younger woman dances her own solos on the strength of it and is discovered city by city. Within the year the arrangement is over and the two women have gone cold on each other, for reasons neither of them ever wrote down.
suggested_refs: The 1902 Fuller company tour of Germany and Austria-Hungary, which launched Duncan's continental career

stops.name: Vienna, the concerts underwritten
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: only the city is attested. No source consulted names the Carltheater as the venue, and the pin marks it on tradition alone; the month is editorial
stops.campa: The company plays Vienna, where Isadora Duncan's independent concerts are underwritten out of Fuller's receipts. The venue is confirmed by no source consulted and the pin rests on tradition only. Vienna in these years is the capital most ready for what Fuller sells, a city whose painters and architects are already treating ornament, line, and the moving female figure as one problem. Koloman Moser draws her here. The Secession takes the two Americans as confirmation of everything it has been arguing.
suggested_refs: The Vienna Secession's interest in Fuller, including Koloman Moser's drawing of her

stops.name: Budapest, the circuit that made another name
stops.date_confidence: the city is attested as a stop on the Fuller-sponsored tour; no dates or programs survive in the reachable sources and the month is editorial
stops.campa: The tour crosses into Hungary. Budapest sits on a circuit that Fuller's booking and Fuller's name have opened for a dancer who could not have opened it herself, and the audiences that take up Isadora Duncan here are audiences assembled for Loie Fuller. The record of the tour is thin, cities without dates and no programs in the reachable sources. The exchange itself is plain enough: an established star spends her own drawing power on an unknown, at the moment her own style is beginning to date.
suggested_refs: The Central European leg of the 1902 tour, attested by city only

stops.name: Bucharest, the Crown Princess
stops.date_confidence: the meeting in 1902 is attested by English Wikipedia and is not corroborated by the article on Marie of Romania; the month is editorial
stops.campa: In Bucharest she is presented to Crown Princess Marie, an English-born granddaughter of Queen Victoria married into a young Balkan monarchy and bored inside it. The two women recognize each other at once. The friendship runs the rest of Fuller's life on a heavy correspondence, and the court gossip supplies the obvious rumor about it. Marie will one day cross the Atlantic on Fuller's arranging to dedicate a museum on a bluff above the Columbia River that neither woman would have found without the other.
suggested_refs: The Fuller-Marie of Romania correspondence, decades long

stops.name: Rue Lhomond, the Curies say no
stops.date_confidence: the approach to the Curies and their refusal are attested by French Wikipedia; the laboratory address and the exact date are reconstruction. The later legend of radium burns is unattested
stops.campa: She goes to Pierre and Marie Curie with a proposal: a costume treated with radium, a dancer who is her own light source, the last problem of her stagecraft solved by the newest element in the world. They refuse, and explain why. She makes the piece anyway out of the phosphorescent salts she already knows, and some accounts call it the radium dance, a tribute rather than a use. A later legend has the Curies handing her radium that burned her hands. No source supports it, and it is entered here as legend.
suggested_refs: The 'danse du radium', staged as tribute to the Curies' discovery

segments.name: The Book, the Sculptor, the Museum

stops.name: Paris, Quinze ans de ma vie
stops.date_confidence: the publication by F. Juven with an introduction by Anatole France is attested for 1908; the month is not given
stops.campa: She publishes her memoir with F. Juven in Paris, fifteen years of a life set down at forty-six, with an introduction by Anatole France. France writes that she grasps the significance of things that look insignificant, and reports having heard her speak with great subtlety about Curie, Madame Curie, and Rodin. The book is her own account and behaves like one. The discoveries are told as accidents, the patented machinery is called instinct, and the failed melodrama decade before Paris is compressed nearly to nothing.
stops.quote: She is one who is able to grasp the profound significance of things that seem insignificant, and to see the splendour hidden in simple lives.
stops.quote_source: Anatole France, Introduction to Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Project Gutenberg #72257
suggested_refs: Quinze ans de ma vie (Paris: F. Juven, 1908), introduction by Anatole France
sources: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Project Gutenberg #72257

stops.name: Meudon, the letter from Rodin
stops.date_confidence: the letter is dated from Meudon, 19 January 1908, and reproduced verbatim in the memoir; her presence at the studio on that date is not stated
stops.campa: Rodin, whom she has visited at Meudon among the plasters, writes her a letter that she will print in her own book: that she is a woman of genius with all the resources of talent, that she has reawakened the spirit of antiquity and shown the Tanagra figurines in action, and that her creation will be attempted again and again by others. She names him as one of two men in France who have impressed her most. The other one wrote her introduction. The letter is dated from Meudon on the nineteenth of January.
stops.quote: Mme. Loie Fuller, whom I have admired for a number of years, is, to my mind, a woman of genius, with all the resources of talent... She has reawakened the spirit of antiquity, showing the Tanagra figurines in action. Her talent will always be imitated, from now on, and her creation will be reattempted over and over again.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, letter dated Meudon, 19 January 1908, printed in Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Chapter XI, Project Gutenberg #72257
suggested_refs: Rodin's Villa des Brillants at Meudon, and Chapter XI of the memoir, 'A Visit at Rodin's'
sources: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Project Gutenberg #72257

stops.name: London, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life
stops.date_confidence: the London edition by Herbert Jenkins is attested for 1913; the translator is uncredited in that edition and the month is not given
stops.campa: The memoir crosses the Channel as Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life, published by Herbert Jenkins with the translator uncredited. In English it reaches the country where she once failed with Caprice and understudied at the Gaiety, twenty-four years on, as the book of a celebrated woman. Inside it, chapter by chapter, sits the only sustained first-person account of how the Serpentine Dance was made and what she believed light and motion to be. It is also the source of nearly every anecdote later told about her.
suggested_refs: Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life, with Some Account of Her Distinguished Friends (London: Herbert Jenkins, 1913)

stops.name: Maryhill, Washington, the house made into a museum
stops.date_confidence: attested: the turning point at Maryhill came in 1917 with Fuller's visit. Accounts placing this in 1920 correspond to no event
stops.campa: On a bluff above the Columbia River she walks through the unfinished concrete mansion of her friend Sam Hill, a road-builder raising a house for a family that will not come to live in it. She tells him to make it a museum instead, for the public good and for the betterment of French art in the far Northwest of America. He does. The building will stand shut for twenty-three years after her death before it opens to the public, a French museum in sagebrush country because a dancer told a road-builder what to do with his walls.
stops.quote: The panes of glass that let the light through ought to be hidden or veiled just as are the lamps that light theatres, then the objects can be observed without the annoyance of the sparkle of the window.
stops.quote_source: Loïe Fuller on museum lighting, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913), Chapter VI, Project Gutenberg #72257
suggested_refs: Maryhill Museum of Art, Klickitat County, Washington, founded on Fuller's advice

stops.name: Paris, Le Lys de la vie
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1921; the month is not given
stops.campa: With Gab Sorère she directs a silent film, Le Lys de la vie, from a story written by Queen Marie of Romania, with a young René Clair among the players. She is fifty-nine and has moved the whole problem into a medium made of light alone, where no bolt of silk is needed and the image is the thing itself. The three of them, the dancer, the manager who became a director, and the queen who wrote fairy tales, have been in each other's lives for nineteen years by the time the camera turns.
suggested_refs: Le Lys de la vie (1921), directed by Loïe Fuller and Gab Sorère, from a story by Marie of Romania

stops.name: Paris, the Legion of Honour and Visions des rêves
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the 1924 decoration comes from general biographical accounts and was not confirmed against a named source in this pass; the ceremony location is unknown and the pin is approximate. The film Visions des rêves is attested for 1924
stops.campa: France decorates her. The Legion of Honour goes to an American who arrived in 1892 with no French and one act, and who has since supplied French poster art, French sculpture, and French theatre with a body they could not stop drawing. The location of the ceremony is not confirmed in the reachable sources. In the same year she makes Visions des rêves, another film built out of the projected light she spent three decades persuading theatres to install for her.
suggested_refs: Visions des rêves (1924); the Légion d'honneur awarded for services to French theatrical art
sources: general biographical accounts of the 1924 decoration, not independently verified in this pass

stops.name: Maryhill, the Queen dedicates the museum
stops.date_confidence: the dedication date and Fuller's organization of the committee behind Marie's American tour are attested; Fuller's own attendance on the bluff is not confirmed
stops.campa: Queen Marie of Romania crosses America by rail to dedicate the museum above the Columbia, an unfinished concrete box in sagebrush country, and gives it more than a hundred objects out of her own household. Fuller assembled the committee that made the royal tour possible, though whether she stands on the bluff that day is not confirmed in the reachable sources. The doors will not open to the public until 1940. The queen, the dancer, and the road-builder will all be dead before anyone buys a ticket.
suggested_refs: The dedication of Maryhill Museum of Art, 3 November 1926, opened to the public 13 May 1940

stops.name: Paris, Les Incertitudes de Coppélius
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1927; the month is not given
stops.campa: Her last film, Les Incertitudes de Coppélius, is made in her sixty-fifth year out of the same materials as everything else: light thrown across moving cloth, and a story about a maker who cannot tell the made thing from the living one. The great serpentine years are thirty-five years behind her. The dance itself has passed into the common stock of vaudeville, performed nightly by women who never heard her name, under machinery she patented and could not defend in any court that would hear her.
suggested_refs: Les Incertitudes de Coppélius (1927), her final film

stops.name: 25 avenue Montaigne, the last days of a year
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia gives 1 January 1928 and the French infobox agrees, while the French running text gives 2 January at the Plaza Athénée in the 8th arrondissement. The contradiction is internal to the French source and is left standing
stops.campa: She dies of pneumonia in the eighth arrondissement, two weeks short of her sixty-sixth birthday. The French article gives the address as 25 avenue Montaigne, beside the Plaza Athénée; its infobox dates the death to the first of January and its own running text to the second, a contradiction inside a single source that is left standing here. The English article gives the first. A woman who spent thirty-six years making light behave dies indoors, in the dark season, in the opening days of a year.
suggested_refs: 25 avenue Montaigne, Paris 8e, given by French Wikipedia as the place of death

stops.name: Père-Lachaise, niche number 5382
stops.date_confidence: the cremation and the niche number are attested; no date is given for the interment and the day here is editorial. The pin marks the Formigé crematorium and columbarium building in the southeast quarter of the cemetery
stops.campa: She is cremated, and the ashes are placed in the columbarium at Père-Lachaise, niche number 5382, inside the building Formigé raised over the cemetery's crematorium. No inscription or memorial text for the niche is recorded in the reachable sources. Almost nothing of what made her famous can be kept: not the timing, not the colour, not the machinery running under the boards. What survives her is the paper, the tinted films of other women, and a great deal of bronze.
suggested_refs: The columbarium of Père-Lachaise, Jean-Camille Formigé's crematorium building of 1894, niche 5382

stops.name: New York, the papers in the Dance Division
stops.date_confidence: the holdings are attested; the date marks the founding of the collection rather than any event in her life
stops.campa: Her manuscripts and papers come to rest in the Jerome Robbins Dance Division of the New York Public Library, in the city where the Serpentine Dance was named and where a court told her she did not own it. The archive holds the residue of work that existed only while the current was on: patents, letters, programs, and photographs of a woman lost inside a cloud of silk, taken by people whose plates could not record the colour the audience had come for.
suggested_refs: Jerome Robbins Dance Division, New York Public Library for the Performing Arts

stops.name: Cannes, La Danseuse on the screen
stops.date_confidence: attested: premiered at Cannes 13 May 2016, released in France 28 September 2016
stops.campa: A French film about her life premieres at Cannes, with Soko as Fuller and Lily-Rose Depp as Isadora Duncan, and opens in France that autumn. The French article says she was practically forgotten by the general public after her death, which is true and is also not the whole account, since in dance history and in the study of Art Nouveau she never left the first page. The film puts an actress in the silk under coloured lamps and sells the image, which is what every theatre and every studio has done with her since 1892.
suggested_refs: La Danseuse (The Dancer, 2016), directed by Stéphanie Di Giusto
